blocks.prompt: 1 (i) Which of the following differential equations are separable and which of them are homogeneous? \(x\frac{dy}{dx} = 1 + y\)
blocks.explanation:
A classification question: we do not solve, we only decide the type.
Divide by \(x\) to get \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) alone, then test the right side for a product \(g(x)h(y)\) and for the ratio \(\frac{y}{x}\).
steps:
Given: \(x\frac{dy}{dx} = 1 + y\).
To find: separable or homogeneous.
Method: write the equation as \(\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x, y)\). If \(f\) factors as (function of \(x\) only) \(\times\) (function of \(y\) only), it is separable. If \(f\) can be written using the ratio \(\frac{y}{x}\) only, it is homogeneous.

Write \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) alone
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1 + y}{x}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{x} \cdot (1 + y)\]
Why: divide both sides by \(x\) (\(x \ne 0\)).

Separable test
\[g(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}, \quad h(y) = 1 + y\]
Why: the right side is a product of a function of \(x\) only and a function of \(y\) only. So the equation is separable: \(\frac{dy}{1 + y} = \frac{dx}{x}\).

Homogeneous test
\[\dfrac{1 + y}{x} = \dfrac{1}{x} + \dfrac{y}{x}\]
Why: the term \(\frac{1}{x}\) cannot be written with \(\frac{y}{x}\) alone (the terms 1 and \(y\) have different degrees), so it is not homogeneous.

blocks.prompt: 1 (ii) Which of the following differential equations are separable and which of them are homogeneous? \(x^2(2y + 1)\,dy - dx = 0\)
blocks.explanation:
Again only the type is asked.
Move \(dx\) across, solve for \(\frac{dy}{dx}\), and look at the right side.
steps:
Given: \(x^2(2y + 1)\,dy - dx = 0\).
To find: separable or homogeneous.
Method: write the equation as \(\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x, y)\). If \(f\) factors as (function of \(x\) only) \(\times\) (function of \(y\) only), it is separable. If \(f\) can be written using the ratio \(\frac{y}{x}\) only, it is homogeneous.

Write \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) alone
\[x^2(2y + 1)\,dy = dx\]
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{x^2(2y + 1)}\]
Why: move \(-dx\) to the right, then divide by \(x^2(2y + 1)\,dx\).

Separable test
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{x^2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2y + 1}\]
Why: a function of \(x\) only times a function of \(y\) only, so separable: \((2y + 1)\,dy = \frac{dx}{x^2}\). (This is Example 6 of 4.2.1.)

Homogeneous test
The denominator \(2x^2y + x^2\) has terms of degree 3 and 2.
Why: unequal degrees, so \(x\) does not cancel after \(y = vx\); not homogeneous.

blocks.prompt: 1 (iii) Which of the following differential equations are separable and which of them are homogeneous? \((2xy + x^2)\,dy - y^2\,dx = 0\)
blocks.explanation:
Only the type is asked.
Solve for \(\frac{dy}{dx}\); then check the degrees of all terms. Equal degrees point to homogeneous.
steps:
Given: \((2xy + x^2)\,dy - y^2\,dx = 0\).
To find: separable or homogeneous.
Method: write the equation as \(\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x, y)\). If \(f\) factors as (function of \(x\) only) \(\times\) (function of \(y\) only), it is separable. If \(f\) can be written using the ratio \(\frac{y}{x}\) only, it is homogeneous.

Write \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) alone
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{y^2}{2xy + x^2}\]
Why: move \(-y^2\,dx\) to the right and divide by \((2xy + x^2)\,dx\).

Homogeneous test
Every term \(y^2\), \(2xy\), \(x^2\) has degree 2. Divide top and bottom by \(x^2\):
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^2}{2\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) + 1}\]
\[= F\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)\]
Why: the right side now uses \(\frac{y}{x}\) only, so the equation is homogeneous.

Separable test
\[\dfrac{y^2}{x(2y + x)}\]
Why: the bracket \(2y + x\) mixes both variables (a sum), so the right side cannot be split into \(g(x)h(y)\); not separable.

blocks.prompt: 1 (iv) Which of the following differential equations are separable and which of them are homogeneous? \(\frac{dy}{dx} = e^{x - y}\)
blocks.explanation:
Only the type is asked.
Use the law of exponents to split \(e^{x - y}\), then test both types.
steps:
Given: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = e^{x - y}\).
To find: separable or homogeneous.
Method: write the equation as \(\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x, y)\). If \(f\) factors as (function of \(x\) only) \(\times\) (function of \(y\) only), it is separable. If \(f\) can be written using the ratio \(\frac{y}{x}\) only, it is homogeneous.

Split the exponential
\[e^{x - y} = e^x \cdot e^{-y}\]
Why: \(a^{m - n} = a^m \cdot a^{-n}\).

Separable test
\[g(x) = e^x, \quad h(y) = e^{-y}\]
Why: a product of a function of \(x\) only and a function of \(y\) only, so separable: \(e^y\,dy = e^x\,dx\).

Homogeneous test
\[x - y = x\left(1 - \dfrac{y}{x}\right)\]
Why: an \(x\) is left outside, so \(e^{x - y}\) cannot be written using \(\frac{y}{x}\) alone; not homogeneous.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key (its item 2, which belongs to Question 1) lists (iv) under "Homogeneous". This is wrong: \(e^{x - y} = e^x \cdot e^{-y}\) is a product \(g(x)h(y)\), so (iv) is separable, and it is not homogeneous.

blocks.prompt: 1 (v) Which of the following differential equations are separable and which of them are homogeneous? \(\frac{dT}{dt} + k(T - T_m) = 0\)
blocks.explanation:
Only the type is asked. Here the variables are \(t\) (independent) and \(T\) (dependent); \(k\) and \(T_m\) are constants.
Solve for \(\frac{dT}{dt}\) and test the right side.
steps:
Given: \(\frac{dT}{dt} + k(T - T_m) = 0\), with \(k\), \(T_m\) constants.
To find: separable or homogeneous.
Method: write \(\frac{dT}{dt} = f(t, T)\). If \(f\) factors as (function of \(t\)) \(\times\) (function of \(T\)), it is separable; if it uses only \(\frac{T}{t}\), it is homogeneous.

Write \(\frac{dT}{dt}\) alone
\[\dfrac{dT}{dt} = -k(T - T_m)\]
Why: move \(k(T - T_m)\) to the right.

Separable test
\[\dfrac{dT}{T - T_m} = -k\,dt\]
Why: the right side is (the constant function \(-k\) of \(t\)) \(\times\) (\(T - T_m\), a function of \(T\) only), so the variables separate. (This is Newton's law of cooling from 4.1.1.)

Homogeneous test
Why: \(T - T_m\) contains no \(t\) at all and the constant \(T_m\) has degree 0 while \(T\) has degree 1, so it cannot be written as a function of \(\frac{T}{t}\); not homogeneous.

blocks.prompt: 1 (vi) Which of the following differential equations are separable and which of them are homogeneous? \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \ln(x) - \ln(y)\); \(x > 0,\ y > 0\)
blocks.explanation:
Only the type is asked.
Combine the two logarithms into one, then see whether the result depends on \(\frac{y}{x}\) only.
steps:
Given: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \ln x - \ln y\), \(x > 0\), \(y > 0\).
To find: separable or homogeneous.
Method: write the equation as \(\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x, y)\). If \(f\) factors as (function of \(x\) only) \(\times\) (function of \(y\) only), it is separable. If \(f\) can be written using the ratio \(\frac{y}{x}\) only, it is homogeneous.

Combine the logarithms
\[\ln x - \ln y = \ln\dfrac{x}{y}\]
\[= -\ln\dfrac{y}{x}\]
Why: \(\ln a - \ln b = \ln\frac{a}{b}\) and \(\ln\frac{x}{y} = -\ln\frac{y}{x}\).

Homogeneous test
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\ln\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right) = F\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)\]
Why: the right side uses \(\frac{y}{x}\) only, so the equation is homogeneous. (With \(y = vx\): \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = -\ln v\).)

Separable test
Why: \(\ln x - \ln y\) is a difference of a function of \(x\) and a function of \(y\), not a product \(g(x)h(y)\); not separable. (Compare \(e^{\ln x - \ln y} = \frac{x}{y}\), which would be separable; the logarithm itself is not.)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key prints "Separable: (i), (ii), (v), (vi)  Homogeneous: (iii), (iv), (vii)". The question has only six parts, so there is no (vii), and two parts are misclassified: (iv) is separable and (vi) is homogeneous (\(\ln x - \ln y = -\ln\frac{y}{x}\)). Correct: separable (i), (ii), (iv), (v); homogeneous (iii), (vi).
